item.title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature — Thu Sep 24 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past

item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment — Thu Sep 24 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment examines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU

item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers — Thu Sep 24 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence) Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers

item.title: Declaration of Independence exhibition grand re-opening — Thu Sep 24, 4:00 PM — ids@iu.edu
item.description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to an opening event on September 24, 2026, celebrating the expansion of our exhibition The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment, newly joined by The Signers in our South Gallery. We welcome IU Associate Professor of History Konstantin Dierks, who will give a lecture entitled "The Declaration in a Time of Crisis." How do people meet the moment in times of political crisis? The Declaration of Independence tried to meet the crisis of 1776. It pinned blame on King George III. It inspired enough colonists to rebel against a mighty empire. It put enduring ideals into American history. The Declaration managed to do so surrounded by a crisis-and before a future-far beyond its grasp. How might we think, then, of the issues we face in 2026? Professor Dierks' talk will be followed by a reception with exhibition curators and seasonal refreshments. item.title: African Studies Colloquium Series — Thu Sep 24, 4:30 PM — Hamilton Lugar School of Global and International Studies (HLS/GISB)
item.description: Juju or Medicine?Discourses of African Traditional Medicine in Jamie Vardy's "Juju Cream" Story and Social Media Reactions Dr. Matthew Ajibade Visiting Lecturer of Yorùbá African Studies Program, Indiana University BloomingtonAbout the Talk This presentation examines how African traditional medicine is framed and contested through Jamie Vardy's recent "juju cream" story involving his former Nigerian Leicester City teammates and the social media reactions that followed. It explores the competing ways African healing practices are characterized and what these responses reveal about broader perceptions of African traditional medicine and the cultural assumptions that shape them.About the Speaker Dr. Matthew Ajibade is a Visiting Lecturer of Yorùbá in the African Studies Program at Indiana University Bloomington. item.title: Kafe Kreyòl — Thu Sep 24, 5:30 PM — Hamilton Lugar School
item.description:
Join us for the first Kafe Kreyòl of the semester! We will explore Kreyòl language varieties, with a focus on Haitian Creole, Martinican Creole, and Louisiana Creole. This gathering will also feature a Kreyòl Show and Tell. Bring a piece of art or media—such as a book, photograph, song, video, artwork, or another meaningful item—to share with the group. Come learn, listen, practice, and connect in a welcoming environment while enjoying coffee, tea, and light refreshments. All experience levels are welcome, and everyone is invited!

item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment — Wed Sep 30 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment examines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU

item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers — Wed Sep 30 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence) Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. item.title: Conversations in Bloom: A Symposium on Art, Community, and Memory — Wed Sep 30, 9:00 AM — I Fell Gallery and Studios; FAR Center for Contemporary Arts; Lotus Education and Arts Foundation
item.description:
The essential goal of Conversations in Bloom: A Symposium on Art, Community, and Memory is to create a community forum for talking about community-making through the arts in Bloomington. The conceptual anchors of the program are arts, community, and memory, which serve as through-lines for thinking about the interplay between shared and individual experiences, work, and histories. Conversation and collaboration are the beating hearts of this program. All of the sessions and events were designed in collaboration with participating community partners over many months of intentional conversation and dialogue. Throughout the planning we pushed ourselves and our community partners to critically examine how our engagement with the arts helps us process the world around us and collectively produce a sense of community and animates memory in ways that help build towards shared futures. We look forward to continuing the conversation with you all.
Source: Visit Bloomington, WFIU Community Calen

item.title: ACES Horizon Talk: Book Talk with Dr. Eveline Washul — Wed Sep 30, 12:00 PM — GLOBAL & INTERNATIONAL STUDIES BUILDING
item.description: Dr. Eveline Washul will discuss her new book, High Lands, Pure Earth: Place Making, History, and Urban Transitions on the Tibetan Plateau (Cornell 2026). In the twenty-first century, China's accelerated urbanization has transformed the Tibetan Plateau. Yet Tibetan urban experiences continue to be profoundly shaped by senses of being in the world that long predate Tibet's subjugation into the modern Chinese nation-state. Combining novel analysis of Tibetan textual sources, ethnographic research, and Indigenous studies frameworks, Washul's book explores how Tibetans actively engage history, peoplehood, and place to build belonging and community even in urban spaces characterized by intense state-led development and assimilation.Please note that this event will be in person only. There will not be a Zoom or hybrid option. item.title: Ostrom Workshop | Research Series: Anasthascia Boateng — Wed Sep 30, 1:00 PM — The Ostrom Workshop
item.description: Bio Anasthascia Boateng is a fourth-year Ph.D. student in the Department of Anthropology. Her research examines how African international students in the United States navigate transnational care, resource sharing, and family obligations within diasporic communities. Drawing on economic anthropology, migration studies, and diaspora philanthropy, she examines the concept of "Black Tax," the expectation that individuals who achieve educational or economic mobility provide support to family and community members across borders. As an Ostrom research awardee and fellow, she investigates how informal institutions, collective action, and shared obligations shape students' everyday lives and contribute to broader conversations about governance, reciprocity, and social support in transnational settings.Title "Black Tax": Diaspora Philanthropy or Burden? item.title: Such Now the Necessity: The Declaration and Secession Symposium — Fri Oct 2, 10:00 AM — INDIANA MEMORIAL UNION (UNION BUILDING)
item.description: The symposium "Such Now the Necessity: The Declaration and Secession" is scheduled for 2 October, from 10:00am to 3:00pm, in the IMU Federal Room. The symposium considers the Declaration specifically as a secessionist document: how it functioned in the early United States, how it relates to broader theories of secession, and how it has been or might be used in other political contexts. The Declaration of Independence is revered as the formative expression of American values. However, it was designed primarily as a legal and rhetorical address to the world—"to the opinions of mankind"—justifying a radical project: secession. The Declaration advances the two principal arguments that are familiar justifications used by secession movements today: an inherent right to self-government based on "consent of the governed," and "remedial secession" in response to "a long train of abuses." item.title: Lecture: "Lessons from a Rapid-Response Web-Archiving Effort"with Anna Kijas — Fri Oct 2, 2:00 PM — Hamilton Lugar School of Global and International Studies
item.description: Anna E. Kijas is Assistant Director of Digital Scholarship and Lilly Music Library at Tufts University. She co-founded Saving Ukrainian Cultural Heritage Online, an initiative focused on safeguarding and preserving the digital cultural heritage of Ukraine during the Russo-Ukrainian War. Anna's work is centered on principles of social justice, access, and sustainability in relation to digital humanities, historical (music) research, cultural heritage, and information studies. Her recent publications include a special issue, "Cultural Heritage in Crisis," for the journal Library Trends, a co-authored chapter, "Nimble Tents and Bunkers: The Role of Libraries in Rapid-Response DH," in The Routledge Companion to Libraries, Archives, and the Digital Humanities, a book entitled The Life and Music of Teresa Carreño (1853-1917): A Guide to Research, and open-access digital projects, including Documenting Teresa Carreño and Rebalancing the Music Canon.
